input.query: Compare metric-learning approaches for few-shot image classification.

claim_records.text: The deep K-tuplet network extends the classical triplet network from deep metric learning for few-shot learning, utilizing the relationship among input samples to learn a general representation via episode-training.

The trained deep K-tuplet network can extract discriminative features for unseen novel categories and can be seamlessly incorporated with a non-linear distance metric function to facilitate few-shot classification.
The proposed method's result on the miniImageNet benchmark outperforms other metric-based few-shot classification methods.

When evaluated on Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs and Stanford Cars using the model trained with miniImageNet, the proposed method significantly outperforms prior methods, demonstrating superior capability to generalize to unseen classes.

The deep K-tuplet Network generalizes the triplet network to allow joint comparison with K negative samples in each mini-batch, making the feature embedding learning process more faithful to the few-shot classification problem with improved feature generalization.
The semi-hard mining sampling technique is an effective sampling strategy to sample informative hard triplets, which can speed up convergence and stabilize the training procedure.
The proposed method outperforms other metric-based methods and achieves competitive performance over other meta-based methods on the miniImageNet dataset.

The proposed method establishes a new experimental setting for evaluating the cross-domain generalization ability for few-shot classification algorithms, and its generalized results on CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, Stanford Cars and Caltech-101 excel other methods.

The proposed method performs target tasks based entirely on feed-forward without requiring further parameter updates, unlike meta-learning methods that need to fine-tune or update parameters for new unseen tasks.

claim_records.text: The proposed Proto-Triplet Loss is based on the original triplet loss with modifications needed to better work on few-shot scenarios.
The proposed ICNN loss is based on an inter and intra class nearest neighbors score, which helps assess the quality of embeddings obtained from the trained network.
The proposed loss functions achieve a significant improvement in accuracy in the miniImageNet benchmark compared to other metric-based few-shot learning methods by a margin of 2%.
The proposed methods demonstrate competitive generalization capabilities to other domains, including Caltech, CUB, Dogs and Cars datasets, compared with the state of the art.
The ICNN Loss measures the intra and inter class distances of batch points and assigns each data point an Inter and Intra Class Nearest Neighbors score.
The Proto-Triplet loss takes a query point as anchor, the prototype from the same class as positive point and the nearest prototype of different class as the negative point.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 61.32% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 79.93% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 60.79% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 80.41% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
The accuracy results of the proposed loss functions on Mini-Imagenet represent an improvement of about 2% compared to the state of the art.
The proposed methods are further tested on the CUB, Caltech, Stanford Dogs and Stanford Cars datasets to assess generalization capabilities, obtaining satisfactory results.

claim_records.text: The proposed Metric-Agnostic Conditional network (MACO) architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Caltech-UCSD birds fine-grained classification task.

The MACO architecture replaces the metric space comparison used in traditional metric-learning few-shot approaches with a learned neural network architecture, outputting a softmax probability distribution rather than a true distance or similarity metric.
The MACO network achieves its best performance only when it is allowed to condition each class representation based on the target (query) image.
The MACO network consists of four distinct stages trained fully end-to-end: a feature stage, a relational stage, a conditioning stage, and a classifier stage.

The MACO feature stage uses a convolutional architecture identical to that of Ravi & Larochelle (2017), composed of four convolutional blocks each with a 3×3 kernel, 32 filters, batch normalization, ELU activation, and 2×2 max pooling, followed by a linear layer producing an 800-dimensional image representation vector.

The MACO relational stage uses a relational network to perform pairwise comparisons of images within each support set class, producing a single order-insensitive vector representation for the class, with parameters shared across all classes.
Traditional metric-learning few-shot approaches place new categories within a learned metric space, most often using a pre-defined distance metric such as Euclidean or cosine distance.

claim_records.text: The proposed Meta-Metric-Learner hybrid model combines optimization-based and metric-based meta-learning approaches, consisting of a task-specific metric-based learner as a base model and a meta-learner that learns and specifies the base model.
The Meta-Metric-Learner model is able to handle flexible numbers of classes as well as generate more generalized metrics for classification across tasks.

Experiments show the Meta-Metric-Learner approach obtains superior performance in both the standard k-shot N-way few-shot learning setting and a new realistic few-shot setting with flexible class numbers in both single-source and multi-source forms.

Existing optimization-based meta-learning approaches require task-specific classifiers to be homogeneous-structured to ease parameter prediction, and thus can only handle few-shot learning problems where tasks share a uniform number of classes.
Existing metric-based meta-learning approaches learn one task-invariant metric for all tasks, and require tasks to come from a similar domain such that a uniform metric works across tasks.

In the Meta-Metric-Learner, the meta learner operating across tasks uses an optimization-based meta-model to discover good parameters and gradient descent in task-specific base learners, while the base learner exploits a metric-based model and parameterizes task metrics using weight prediction from the optimization-based meta-learner.

The Meta-Metric-Learner is able to handle unbalanced classes in meta-train and meta-test sets, and generates task-specific metrics leveraging weight prediction from the meta-learner given task instances.

Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) explicitly trains initial parameters of a CNN model such that a small number of gradient update steps with a small amount of training data from a new task will produce good generalization performance on that task.

claim_records.text: The proposed adaptive metric learning approach automatically determines the best weighted combination from a set of metrics obtained from meta-training tasks for a newly seen few-shot task.

Extensive quantitative evaluations on real-world sentiment analysis and dialog intent classification datasets demonstrate that the proposed method performs favorably against state-of-the-art few-shot learning algorithms in terms of predictive accuracy.

The proposed task-clustering framework for diverse few-shot learning includes an initial task clustering algorithm based on matrix completion, followed by a few-shot learning method based on task clustering.
Directly using transfer performance for task clustering requires O(n²) source-target transfer learning evaluations, where n is the number of meta-training tasks.
For large numbers of diverse meta-training tasks where n exceeds 1000, evaluating the full transfer performance matrix is unacceptable as it requires over 1 million entries to evaluate.
The proposed matrix completion-based task clustering algorithm addresses efficiency challenges by randomly sampling task pairs to evaluate S_ij and S_ji transfer performance scores.
The proposed matrix completion-based task clustering algorithm addresses unreliable entries and asymmetry issues by keeping only task pairs (i, j) with consistent S_ij and S_ji scores.

Most previous few-shot learning works employ a common meta-model (metric-based or optimization-based) for all few-shot tasks because tasks are sampled from a single domain such as Omniglot or ImageNet.
In enterprise AI cloud service scenarios, client-submitted text classification tasks are significantly diverse, making a common metric insufficient to handle all tasks.

Few-shot learning aims to learn classifiers from few examples per class, with deep learning approaches learning meta-models from a large number of meta-training tasks for rapid adaptation to target tasks with few training examples.

claim_records.text: Deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification classify unseen samples according to their distances to few seen samples in an embedding space learned by deep neural networks, avoiding overfitting to few training images and achieving state-of-the-art performance.

The review categorizes deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification from 2018 to 2022 into three groups according to three stages of metric learning: learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance measures.

In few-shot classification, the metric is learned on the base dataset, and query images of novel classes are classified by computing their distances to novel support images with respect to the learned measure, followed by a distance-based classifier such as k-nearest neighbors.

fact_fields.method: Supervised metric learning for few-shot classification

claim_records.text: Early few-shot metric learning methods such as Siamese Network and Matching Network classify a query sample by measuring and comparing its distance to support samples.

claim_records.text: The Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot (UAFS) framework models uncertainty of query-prototype similarity and performs uncertainty-aware optimization for image classification.

Rather than using a scalar, the similarity between a query feature zi and a prototype feature cj is modeled by a distribution (probabilistic similarity) based on graph-based similarity uncertainty estimation.
For a query sample xi and N prototypes in the support set, each query-prototype pair is treated as a node and a graph-based model jointly infers the similarity uncertainty σi,j for each pair.

fact_fields.method: Graph-based model for joint similarity uncertainty inference

claim_records.text: The network is optimized with similarity-based classification losses that exploit the estimated similarity uncertainty.
The proposed Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot framework converts observed similarities to probabilistic representations and incorporates them into the loss for more effective optimization.
A graph-based model is utilized to estimate the uncertainty of query-support pair similarities in the proposed framework.
Extensive experiments show the proposed method brings significant improvements on top of a strong baseline and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

In few-shot image classification, the set of category-specific prototypes (averaged support sample feature embeddings) acts as a similarity-based classifier to identify a query sample's category by finding the nearest prototype in the embedding space.
During training, a query sample's logit vector (classification probability) is obtained by feeding similarities between the query sample and prototypes to a SoftMax function.

For each query-prototype pair, the observed feature similarity between the query and prototype is converted from a deterministic scalar to a distribution, with the distribution's variance characterizing the uncertainty of the observed similarity.
Aleatoric uncertainty identifies the confidence level of the network on its output for a sample, capturing noise inherent in the observations.

For few-shot image classification, the network has different uncertainties on calculated similarities of different query-prototype pairs, and higher uncertainty corresponds to less reliable estimated similarity.

claim_records.text: A learning-to-learn approach is applied to search for the hyper-parameters of the feature-wise transformation layers to capture variations of feature distributions under different domains.
Extensive experiments and ablation studies under the domain generalization setting use five few-shot classification datasets: mini-ImageNet, CUB, Cars, Places, and Plantae.
The proposed feature-wise transformation layer is applicable to various metric-based models and provides consistent improvements on few-shot classification performance under domain shift.

claim_records.text: Region Comparison Network (RCN) is a metric learning based method proposed for interpretable few-shot image classification, designed to reveal how few-shot learning works in a neural network and identify mutually related regions between query and support set images.
Region Activation Mapping (RAM) is a visualization strategy designed to intuitively explain what RCN has learned by visualizing intermediate variables in the network.
The interpretability of RCN can be generalized from the task level to the category level, which corresponds to identifying prototypical parts that support the final classification decision of RCN.
Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that RCN outperforms existing baselines for few-shot image classification.

RCN's final prediction module learns a generated weight of regions to explain which regions in a support sample are similar to locations in a query sample and which regions the model prefers to compare.
RCN is designed to generate a region weight in the final stage to define which common parts between support and query samples most influence the final similarity score.
Existing few-shot learning works are grouped into metric-based models (e.g., matching networks, prototypical networks) and gradient-based models (e.g., MAML, MetaSGD).

fact_fields.method: Categorization of existing few-shot learning methods

claim_records.text: RCN's region meta learner functions as a dynamic system that adapts to different meta tasks during both training and testing stages.

claim_records.text: MF-Adapter is a proposed method that combines complementary strengths of low-level local representations (LRs) and high-level semantic representations for CLIP-based few-shot image classification.
Meta-Feature Unit (MF-Unit) is a simple yet effective local similarity metric designed to measure category-consistent local context in an inductive manner.
MF-Adapter is trained to map image features to MF-Unit to generalize intra-class knowledge between unseen images and the support set.
Extensive experiments show MF-Adapter outperforms state-of-the-art CLIP downstream few-shot classification methods, including on challenging visual classification tasks.

MF-Unit is obtained by inductive representation of local feature maps on different scales using sliding windows with different perceptual fields, containing rich local information representing category-consistent characteristics.
MF-Unit is calculated via inductive max and mean operations on each sliding window to compress parameters and reduce redundancy, representing category-consistent features with inductive knowledge.

During inference, MF-Adapter first infers test images into MF-Units at different levels and scales, retrieves few-shot knowledge in the MF-Unit space of the support set to get local logits, then combines this with the original CLIP high-level prediction for the final prediction.
MF-Adapter achieves state-of-the-art performance across 11 widely adopted datasets for few-shot classification, and is the first work to utilize the local similarity of CLIP in few-shot learning.

In few-shot classification scenarios with insufficient seen images, the standard pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm for CLIP does not produce improved results, so common practice is to fix CLIP pre-training weights and learn a lightweight adaptation module.
Tip-Adapter achieves large performance improvements over both prompt-based methods and CLIP-Adapter on several classification datasets by fine-tuning a trainable query-key cache layer on top of CLIP.

Extending prototypical networks to zero-shot learning achieves state-of-the-art results on the CU-Birds dataset.

claim_records.text: The proposed subspace representation learning (SRL) framework represents an image using a subspace in local CNN feature space and measures similarity between two images via a weighted subspace distance (WSD).
When K images are available per class, the SRL framework develops two types of template subspaces to aggregate K-shot information: the prototypical subspace (PS) and the discriminative subspace (DS).
The SRL framework extends metric learning based techniques from vector to subspace representation.
Using subspace representation instead of the previously adopted global vector representation can effectively preserve the spatial structure and diversity within an image.

fact_fields.method: subspace representation vs global vector representation

claim_records.text: Experimental results on three public benchmark datasets (MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB)) demonstrate competitive or superior performance of the SRL method compared to previous state-of-the-art approaches.

claim_records.text: Metric-based few-shot image classification directly measures relations between query images and support classes to learn transferable feature embeddings.
Previous work using image-level feature representations cannot effectively estimate a class's distribution due to the scarcity of samples.
Local descriptor based representations can achieve richer representations than image-level based representations.

Existing local descriptor based few-shot learning works still rely on a less effective instance-level metric, especially a symmetric metric, to measure relations between query images and support classes.
An asymmetric measure is argued to be more suitable for metric-based few-shot learning given the natural asymmetric relation between a query image and a support class.

fact_fields.method: asymmetric measure for metric-based few-shot learning

claim_records.text: The proposed Asymmetric Distribution Measure (ADM) network calculates a joint local and global asymmetric measure between two multivariate local distributions of queries and classes for few-shot learning.
A task-aware Contrastive Measure Strategy (CMS) is proposed to further enhance the measure function in the ADM network.
On miniImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 3.02% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.
On tieredImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 1.56% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.

claim_records.text: RankDNN casts relevance ranking for image retrieval as binary ranking relation classification.
Ranking relation classification is sample efficient and domain agnostic in comparison to image classification.
The core component of RankDNN is a simple MLP that takes as input an image triplet encoded as the difference between two vector-Kronecker products, and outputs a binary relevance ranking order.
RankMLP can be built on top of any state-of-the-art feature extractors.
RankDNN can be flexibly fused with other post-processing methods.
During meta test, RankDNN ranks support images according to their similarity with the query samples, and each query sample is assigned the class label of its nearest neighbor.
RankDNN can effectively improve the performance of its baselines based on a variety of backbones.
RankDNN outperforms previous state-of-the-art algorithms on multiple few-shot learning benchmarks including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds, and CIFAR-FS.
Experiments on the cross-domain challenge demonstrate the superior transferability of RankDNN.

claim_records.text: The proposed QSFormer model integrates a global query-support sample Transformer (sampleFormer) branch and a local patch Transformer (patchFormer) learning branch to simultaneously address the two core challenges of few-shot classification.

The sampleFormer branch of QSFormer adopts Encoder, Decoder and Cross-Attention to respectively model Support representation, Query image representation, and metric learning for few-shot classification.

The local patch Transformer (patchFormer) branch of QSFormer extracts structural representation for each image sample by capturing the long-range dependence of local image patches, serving as a complement to the global learning branch.
A novel Cross-scale Interactive Feature Extractor (CIFE) is proposed to extract and fuse multi-scale CNN features as an effective backbone module for the QSFormer few-shot learning method.
All modules of QSFormer are integrated into a unified framework and trained in an end-to-end manner.
Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed QSFormer for few-shot classification.

Few-shot classification is typically formulated as a metric learning problem, with core challenges of learning consistent representations for images in support and query sets, and effective metric learning between support and query images.
Few-shot classification aims to recognize unseen classes using very limited samples.

claim_records.text: Traditional metric-based few-shot classification methods typically rely on a single distance value between the query feature and support feature, overlooking the contribution of shallow features.

The proposed method uses a multi-output embedding network that maps samples into distinct feature spaces by extracting feature vectors at different stages, enabling the model to capture both global and abstract features.
Employing a self-attention mechanism improves the refinement of features at each stage, leading to more robust representations and improved overall performance.
Assigning learnable weights to each stage of the multi-output embedding network significantly improved performance and results.
Comprehensive evaluations of the proposed method were conducted on the MiniImageNet and FC100 datasets in the 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot scenarios.
Cross-domain tasks across eight benchmark datasets were performed for the proposed method, achieving high accuracy in the testing domains.
The evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in comparison to state-of-the-art approaches.
The goal of few-shot classification is to train a classifier using a limited number of samples while maintaining satisfactory performance.

fact_fields.method: metric-learning methods for few-shot image classification

claim_records.text: A measure at only the image feature level may not be effective enough to generalize from base to novel classes when using only a few images.
The proposed multi-level correlation network (MLCN) for few-shot image classification effectively captures local information by using a multi-level descriptor of an image.
The self-correlation module and cross-correlation module in MLCN learn the semantic correspondence relation of local information based on learned representations.
The pattern-correlation module in MLCN captures the pattern of fine-grained images and finds relevant structural patterns between base classes and novel classes.
Extensive experiments and analysis show the effectiveness of the proposed MLCN method on four widely-used few-shot image classification benchmarks.

claim_records.text: The proposed approach controls the semantic embedding of images by formulating it as a metric learning problem for zero-shot image classification.

fact_fields.method: metric learning formulation for semantic embedding control

claim_records.text: The optimized empirical criterion of the proposed approach associates two types of sub-task constraints: metric discriminating capacity and accurate attribute prediction.

The resulting zero-shot learning expression does not require the notion of class in the training phase, with only pairs of image/attributes augmented with a consistency indicator given as ground truth.
At test time, the learned model can predict the consistency of a test image with a given set of attributes, allowing flexible ways to produce recognition inferences.
The proposed approach gives state-of-the-art results on four challenging datasets used for zero-shot recognition evaluation.

claim_records.text: ProtoTransfer is a self-supervised transfer learning approach that constructs a metric embedding clustering unlabeled prototypical samples and their augmentations closely together, with the pre-trained embedding serving as a starting point for few-shot classification via class cluster summarization and fine-tuning.
ProtoTransfer outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised meta-learning methods on few-shot tasks from the mini-ImageNet dataset.
In few-shot experiments with realistic domain shift, ProtoTransfer achieves comparable performance to supervised methods while requiring orders of magnitude fewer labels.
Common transfer learning has been shown to outperform supervised meta-learning in settings with realistic domain shift.
Unsupervised meta-learning methods exchange the annotation requirement for a reduction in few-shot classification performance.

claim_records.text: HyperShot is a proposed few-shot learning model that fuses kernels and the hypernetwork paradigm.
Unlike reference approaches that apply a gradient-based adjustment of parameters, HyperShot switches classification module parameters depending on the task's embedding.
HyperShot utilizes a hypernetwork that takes aggregated information from support data and returns classifier parameters handcrafted for the considered problem.
HyperShot introduces a kernel-based representation of support examples delivered to the hypernetwork to create the parameters of the classification module.
HyperShot relies on relations between embeddings of support examples instead of direct feature values provided by backbone models.
The HyperShot approach enables the model to adapt to highly different tasks.

claim_records.text: The proposed Siamese Transformer Network (STN) employs two parallel branch networks utilizing the pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to extract global and local features respectively.
The STN implementation uses the ViT-Small network architecture, with branch networks initialized with pre-trained model parameters obtained through self-supervised learning.
The STN applies Euclidean distance measure to global features and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure to local features.
The STN integrates the two feature metrics by first applying L2 normalization then weighting the normalized results to obtain the final similarity score.
During the training phase, the STN adopts a meta-learning approach to fine-tune the entire network.

Extensive experiments show the STN framework achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on four popular few-shot classification benchmarks in both 5-shot and 1-shot scenarios.

claim_records.text: The proposed Mutual Centralized Learning (MCL) method affiliates two disjoint sets of dense features in a bidirectional paradigm, associating each local feature with a particle that can bidirectionally random walk in a discrete feature space by the affiliations.
MCL estimates class probability via features' accessibility, which measures the expected number of visits to the support features of that class in a Markov process.
MCL relates to learning a centrality on an affiliation network and can be plugged into existing methods by highlighting centralized local features.
Experiments show that the MCL method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both miniImageNet and tieredImageNet.

claim_records.text: The proposed Generative Dual Adversarial Network provides a unified framework for visual->semantic mapping, semantic->visual mapping, and metric learning for generalized zero-shot learning.

The proposed model consists of a feature generator that generates visual features from class embeddings, a regressor that maps visual features back to class embeddings, and a discriminator that evaluates closeness between image features and class embeddings.
All three components of the proposed model are trained under the combination of cyclic consistency loss and dual adversarial loss.
Experimental results show the proposed model preserves higher accuracy in classifying images from seen classes compared to prior approaches.
Experimental results show the proposed model performs better than existing state-of-the-art models in classifying images from unseen classes.

claim_records.text: The proposed patch-driven relational refinement learns cache adapter weights from intra-image patch dependencies rather than treating an image embedding as a monolithic vector.

The introduced relational gated graph attention network constructs a patch graph and performs edge-aware attention to emphasize informative inter-patch interactions, producing context-enriched patch embeddings.
A learnable multi-aggregation pooling composes context-enriched patch embeddings into compact, task-discriminative representations that better align cache keys with the target few-shot classes.
The proposed graph refinement is used only during training to distil relational structure into the cache, incurring no additional inference cost beyond standard cache lookup.
Final predictions are obtained by a residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits.

claim_records.text: Few-shot Cosine Transformer (FS-CT) consists of a learnable prototypical embedding network to obtain categorical representations from support samples with hard cases, and a transformer encoder to effectively achieve the relational map from two different support and query samples.

Cosine Attention, a more robust and stable attention module, enhances the transformer module significantly and improves FS-CT performance from 5% to over 20% in accuracy compared to the default scaled dot-product mechanism.
FS-CT performs competitive results in mini-ImageNet, CUB-200, and CIFAR-FS on 1-shot learning and 5-shot learning tasks across backbones and few-shot configurations.
A custom few-shot dataset for Yoga pose recognition was developed to demonstrate the potential of the FS-CT algorithm for practical application.
FS-CT with cosine attention is a lightweight, simple few-shot algorithm applicable for a wide range of applications such as healthcare, medical, and security surveillance.

claim_records.text: HelixFormer is a Transformer-based double-helix model proposed to achieve cross-image object semantic relation mining in a bidirectional and symmetrical manner for few-shot fine-grained image classification.
HelixFormer consists of two steps: Relation Mining Process (RMP) across different branches, and Representation Enhancement Process (REP) within each individual branch.

The designed RMP in HelixFormer enables each branch to extract fine-grained object-level Cross-image Semantic Relation Maps (CSRMs) using information from the other branch, ensuring better cross-image interaction in semantically related local object regions.

With the aid of CSRMs, the developed REP in HelixFormer strengthens extracted features for discovered semantically-related local regions in each branch, boosting the model's ability to distinguish subtle feature differences of fine-grained objects.

Extensive experiments on five public fine-grained benchmarks demonstrate that HelixFormer achieves much better performance over most state-of-the-art methods under 1-shot and 5-shot few-shot scenarios.
The code for HelixFormer is publicly available at https://github.com/JiakangYuan/HelixFormer.

claim_records.text: In few-shot learning, the conventional pooled global feature is likely to lose useful local characteristics.

Existing deep descriptor-based FSL methods generally take all deep descriptors from neural networks into consideration, ignoring that some descriptors are useless in classification due to their limited receptive field.

The paper argues that a Mutual Nearest Neighbor (MNN) relation should be established to explicitly select query descriptors most relevant to each task and discard less relevant ones from aggregative clutters in FSL.
The proposed method for FSL is Discriminative Mutual Nearest Neighbor Neural Network (DMN4).

fact_fields.method: Discriminative Mutual Nearest Neighbor Neural Network (DMN4)

claim_records.text: Extensive experiments demonstrate that DMN4 outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on both fine-grained and generalized datasets.

claim_records.text: Image background common in realistic images is empirically identified as a shortcut knowledge helpful for in-class classification but ungeneralizable beyond training categories in Few-Shot Learning.
The COSOC framework is designed to tackle the background shortcut problem by extracting foreground objects in images at both training and evaluation without any extra supervision.
Extensive experiments carried on inductive FSL tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the COSOC approach.

claim_records.text: The explored simple transformer-based few-shot learning pipeline yields surprisingly good performance on standard few-shot image classification benchmarks including Mini-ImageNet, CIFAR-FS, CDFSL and Meta-Dataset.

fact_fields.method: Simple transformer-based three-stage pipeline: unsupervised external data pre-training, base category meta-training, novel task fine-tuning

claim_records.text: The three-stage few-shot learning pipeline uses unsupervised external data for pre-training, base categories to simulate few-shot tasks for meta-training, and scarce labeled data from the novel task for fine-tuning.

The study investigates how pre-training on external data benefits few-shot learning, how state-of-the-art transformer architectures can be exploited for few-shot learning, and how fine-tuning mitigates domain shift in few-shot image classification.
The code and demo for the proposed simple transformer-based few-shot learning pipeline are publicly available at https://hushell.github.io/pmf.

claim_records.text: FiT combines fixed pretrained backbones, fine-tuned FiLM adapter layers, automatically configured Naive Bayes classifiers, and episodic training to produce parameter efficient image classification models with superior low-shot classification accuracy.
FiT achieves better classification accuracy than the leading Big Transfer (BiT) algorithm at low-shot across a wide range of downstream datasets.
FiT achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the challenging VTAB-1k benchmark using fewer than 1% of the updateable parameters.

FiT demonstrates parameter efficiency and superior accuracy in distributed low-shot applications including model personalization and federated learning where model update size is an important performance metric.
The parameter efficiency of FiT enables few-shot learning, inexpensive model updates for personalization, and communication efficient federated learning.

claim_records.text: Most current few shot methods train an encoder on a base dataset rich in labeled examples to obtain representations of support instances for novel classes, but test instances from a distribution different to the base distribution have poor feature representation quality that degrades performance.

BaseTransformers attends to the most relevant regions of the base dataset feature space and improves support instance representations by using well-trained feature representations of base dataset points closest to each support instance during meta-test time.
Experiments on three benchmark datasets show that BaseTransformers works well for several backbones and achieves state-of-the-art results in the inductive one shot setting.

claim_records.text: In meta-learning for few-shot classification, the shot number used during meta-training generally should match the shot number used during meta-testing to obtain the best performance.
The paper introduces a theoretical analysis of the impact of shot number on Prototypical Networks, a state-of-the-art few-shot classification method.
The proposed method derived from the theoretical analysis is robust to the choice of shot number used during meta-training, which is identified as a crucial hyperparameter.
The model trained for an arbitrary meta-training shot number shows great performance across different values of meta-testing shot numbers.
The approach is experimentally demonstrated on different few-shot classification benchmarks.

claim_records.text: Prototypical Random Walk Networks (PRWN) is a semi-supervised few-shot learning approach built on top of Prototypical Networks (PN).
The developed random walk semi-supervised loss enables the network to learn representations that are compact and well-separated.

Compact and well-separated class representations can be achieved by modeling the prototypical random walk notion without needing additional graph-NN parameters or requiring a transductive setting where a collective test set is provided.
The PRWN model outperforms baselines in most benchmarks, with significant improvements in some cases.

PRWN trained with 40% of the data as labeled achieves 50.89% accuracy in the 1-shot mini-Imagenet case, outperforming fully supervised Prototypical Networks trained on 100% of the labels which achieves 49.4% accuracy.

fact_fields.method: PRWN vs fully supervised Prototypical Networks

claim_records.text: The PRWN loss is resistant to distractors, which are unlabeled data that do not belong to any of the training classes, reflecting robustness to labeled/unlabeled class distribution mismatch.

claim_records.text: Boundary patches corresponding to pixels located at the boundary of objects in hyperspectral images are hard to classify, as they are mixed with multi-class spectral information.

fact_fields.method: Observation of existing few-shot hyperspectral image classification methods' classification results

claim_records.text: The proposed APNT method takes the prototype network as the backbone and adopts a transformer as feature extractor to learn pixel-to-pixel relation and apply different attentions to different pixels.
APNT randomly mixes up two patches to imitate boundary patches and uses the synthetic patches for training, to enlarge the number of hard training samples and enhance their diversity.
APNT follows the TransMix data augmentation technique, using the attention returned by the transformer to mix up the labels of two patches to generate better labels for synthetic patches.
The proposed APNT method demonstrates state of the art performance and better robustness for few-shot hyperspectral image classification compared with existing methods in experiments.
Few-shot hyperspectral image classification aims to identify the classes of each pixel in hyperspectral images by only marking few of these pixels.

claims: Boundary patches corresponding to pixels located at the boundary of objects in hyperspectral images are hard to classify, as they are mixed with multi-class spectral information.
The proposed APNT method takes the prototype network as the backbone and adopts a transformer as feature extractor to learn pixel-to-pixel relation and apply different attentions to different pixels.
APNT randomly mixes up two patches to imitate boundary patches and uses the synthetic patches for training, to enlarge the number of hard training samples and enhance their diversity.
APNT follows the TransMix data augmentation technique, using the attention returned by the transformer to mix up the labels of two patches to generate better labels for synthetic patches.
The proposed APNT method demonstrates state of the art performance and better robustness for few-shot hyperspectral image classification compared with existing methods in experiments.

claim_records.text: Proto-CLIP is a few-shot learning framework that leverages large-scale vision-language models such as CLIP, utilizing both image prototypes and text prototypes for few-shot learning.
Proto-CLIP adapts the image and text encoder embeddings from CLIP in a joint fashion using few-shot examples.
The embeddings from CLIP's image and text encoders are used to compute the respective prototypes of image classes for classification in Proto-CLIP.

During adaptation, Proto-CLIP aligns the image and text prototypes of corresponding classes, which is beneficial for few-shot classification due to reinforced contributions from both types of prototypes.
Proto-CLIP has both training-free and fine-tuned variants.
The effectiveness of Proto-CLIP is demonstrated by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets for few-shot learning, as well as in the real world for robot perception.

claim_records.text: The deep K-tuplet network extends the classical triplet network from deep metric learning for few-shot learning, utilizing the relationship among input samples to learn a general representation via episode-training.

The trained deep K-tuplet network can extract discriminative features for unseen novel categories and can be seamlessly incorporated with a non-linear distance metric function to facilitate few-shot classification.
The proposed method's result on the miniImageNet benchmark outperforms other metric-based few-shot classification methods.

When evaluated on Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs and Stanford Cars using the model trained with miniImageNet, the proposed method significantly outperforms prior methods, demonstrating superior capability to generalize to unseen classes.

The deep K-tuplet Network generalizes the triplet network to allow joint comparison with K negative samples in each mini-batch, making the feature embedding learning process more faithful to the few-shot classification problem with improved feature generalization.
The semi-hard mining sampling technique is an effective sampling strategy to sample informative hard triplets, which can speed up convergence and stabilize the training procedure.
The proposed method outperforms other metric-based methods and achieves competitive performance over other meta-based methods on the miniImageNet dataset.

The proposed method establishes a new experimental setting for evaluating the cross-domain generalization ability for few-shot classification algorithms, and its generalized results on CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, Stanford Cars and Caltech-101 excel other methods.

The proposed method performs target tasks based entirely on feed-forward without requiring further parameter updates, unlike meta-learning methods that need to fine-tune or update parameters for new unseen tasks.

claim_records.text: The proposed Proto-Triplet Loss is based on the original triplet loss with modifications needed to better work on few-shot scenarios.
The proposed ICNN loss is based on an inter and intra class nearest neighbors score, which helps assess the quality of embeddings obtained from the trained network.
The proposed loss functions achieve a significant improvement in accuracy in the miniImageNet benchmark compared to other metric-based few-shot learning methods by a margin of 2%.
The proposed methods demonstrate competitive generalization capabilities to other domains, including Caltech, CUB, Dogs and Cars datasets, compared with the state of the art.
The ICNN Loss measures the intra and inter class distances of batch points and assigns each data point an Inter and Intra Class Nearest Neighbors score.
The Proto-Triplet loss takes a query point as anchor, the prototype from the same class as positive point and the nearest prototype of different class as the negative point.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 61.32% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 79.93% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 60.79% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 80.41% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
The accuracy results of the proposed loss functions on Mini-Imagenet represent an improvement of about 2% compared to the state of the art.
The proposed methods are further tested on the CUB, Caltech, Stanford Dogs and Stanford Cars datasets to assess generalization capabilities, obtaining satisfactory results.

claim_records.text: The proposed Metric-Agnostic Conditional network (MACO) architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Caltech-UCSD birds fine-grained classification task.

The MACO architecture replaces the metric space comparison used in traditional metric-learning few-shot approaches with a learned neural network architecture, outputting a softmax probability distribution rather than a true distance or similarity metric.
The MACO network achieves its best performance only when it is allowed to condition each class representation based on the target (query) image.
The MACO network consists of four distinct stages trained fully end-to-end: a feature stage, a relational stage, a conditioning stage, and a classifier stage.

The MACO feature stage uses a convolutional architecture identical to that of Ravi & Larochelle (2017), composed of four convolutional blocks each with a 3×3 kernel, 32 filters, batch normalization, ELU activation, and 2×2 max pooling, followed by a linear layer producing an 800-dimensional image representation vector.

The MACO relational stage uses a relational network to perform pairwise comparisons of images within each support set class, producing a single order-insensitive vector representation for the class, with parameters shared across all classes.
Traditional metric-learning few-shot approaches place new categories within a learned metric space, most often using a pre-defined distance metric such as Euclidean or cosine distance.

claim_records.text: The proposed Meta-Metric-Learner hybrid model combines optimization-based and metric-based meta-learning approaches, consisting of a task-specific metric-based learner as a base model and a meta-learner that learns and specifies the base model.
The Meta-Metric-Learner model is able to handle flexible numbers of classes as well as generate more generalized metrics for classification across tasks.

Experiments show the Meta-Metric-Learner approach obtains superior performance in both the standard k-shot N-way few-shot learning setting and a new realistic few-shot setting with flexible class numbers in both single-source and multi-source forms.

Existing optimization-based meta-learning approaches require task-specific classifiers to be homogeneous-structured to ease parameter prediction, and thus can only handle few-shot learning problems where tasks share a uniform number of classes.
Existing metric-based meta-learning approaches learn one task-invariant metric for all tasks, and require tasks to come from a similar domain such that a uniform metric works across tasks.

In the Meta-Metric-Learner, the meta learner operating across tasks uses an optimization-based meta-model to discover good parameters and gradient descent in task-specific base learners, while the base learner exploits a metric-based model and parameterizes task metrics using weight prediction from the optimization-based meta-learner.

The Meta-Metric-Learner is able to handle unbalanced classes in meta-train and meta-test sets, and generates task-specific metrics leveraging weight prediction from the meta-learner given task instances.

Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) explicitly trains initial parameters of a CNN model such that a small number of gradient update steps with a small amount of training data from a new task will produce good generalization performance on that task.

claim_records.text: The proposed adaptive metric learning approach automatically determines the best weighted combination from a set of metrics obtained from meta-training tasks for a newly seen few-shot task.

Extensive quantitative evaluations on real-world sentiment analysis and dialog intent classification datasets demonstrate that the proposed method performs favorably against state-of-the-art few-shot learning algorithms in terms of predictive accuracy.

The proposed task-clustering framework for diverse few-shot learning includes an initial task clustering algorithm based on matrix completion, followed by a few-shot learning method based on task clustering.
Directly using transfer performance for task clustering requires O(n²) source-target transfer learning evaluations, where n is the number of meta-training tasks.
For large numbers of diverse meta-training tasks where n exceeds 1000, evaluating the full transfer performance matrix is unacceptable as it requires over 1 million entries to evaluate.
The proposed matrix completion-based task clustering algorithm addresses efficiency challenges by randomly sampling task pairs to evaluate S_ij and S_ji transfer performance scores.
The proposed matrix completion-based task clustering algorithm addresses unreliable entries and asymmetry issues by keeping only task pairs (i, j) with consistent S_ij and S_ji scores.

Most previous few-shot learning works employ a common meta-model (metric-based or optimization-based) for all few-shot tasks because tasks are sampled from a single domain such as Omniglot or ImageNet.
In enterprise AI cloud service scenarios, client-submitted text classification tasks are significantly diverse, making a common metric insufficient to handle all tasks.

claim_records.text: The Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot (UAFS) framework models uncertainty of query-prototype similarity and performs uncertainty-aware optimization for image classification.

Rather than using a scalar, the similarity between a query feature zi and a prototype feature cj is modeled by a distribution (probabilistic similarity) based on graph-based similarity uncertainty estimation.
For a query sample xi and N prototypes in the support set, each query-prototype pair is treated as a node and a graph-based model jointly infers the similarity uncertainty σi,j for each pair.

fact_fields.method: Graph-based model for joint similarity uncertainty inference

claim_records.text: The network is optimized with similarity-based classification losses that exploit the estimated similarity uncertainty.
The proposed Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot framework converts observed similarities to probabilistic representations and incorporates them into the loss for more effective optimization.
A graph-based model is utilized to estimate the uncertainty of query-support pair similarities in the proposed framework.
Extensive experiments show the proposed method brings significant improvements on top of a strong baseline and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

In few-shot image classification, the set of category-specific prototypes (averaged support sample feature embeddings) acts as a similarity-based classifier to identify a query sample's category by finding the nearest prototype in the embedding space.
During training, a query sample's logit vector (classification probability) is obtained by feeding similarities between the query sample and prototypes to a SoftMax function.

For each query-prototype pair, the observed feature similarity between the query and prototype is converted from a deterministic scalar to a distribution, with the distribution's variance characterizing the uncertainty of the observed similarity.
Aleatoric uncertainty identifies the confidence level of the network on its output for a sample, capturing noise inherent in the observations.

For few-shot image classification, the network has different uncertainties on calculated similarities of different query-prototype pairs, and higher uncertainty corresponds to less reliable estimated similarity.

claim_records.text: Region Comparison Network (RCN) is a metric learning based method proposed for interpretable few-shot image classification, designed to reveal how few-shot learning works in a neural network and identify mutually related regions between query and support set images.
Region Activation Mapping (RAM) is a visualization strategy designed to intuitively explain what RCN has learned by visualizing intermediate variables in the network.
The interpretability of RCN can be generalized from the task level to the category level, which corresponds to identifying prototypical parts that support the final classification decision of RCN.
Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that RCN outperforms existing baselines for few-shot image classification.

RCN's final prediction module learns a generated weight of regions to explain which regions in a support sample are similar to locations in a query sample and which regions the model prefers to compare.
RCN is designed to generate a region weight in the final stage to define which common parts between support and query samples most influence the final similarity score.
Existing few-shot learning works are grouped into metric-based models (e.g., matching networks, prototypical networks) and gradient-based models (e.g., MAML, MetaSGD).

claim_records.text: MF-Adapter is a proposed method that combines complementary strengths of low-level local representations (LRs) and high-level semantic representations for CLIP-based few-shot image classification.
Meta-Feature Unit (MF-Unit) is a simple yet effective local similarity metric designed to measure category-consistent local context in an inductive manner.
MF-Adapter is trained to map image features to MF-Unit to generalize intra-class knowledge between unseen images and the support set.
Extensive experiments show MF-Adapter outperforms state-of-the-art CLIP downstream few-shot classification methods, including on challenging visual classification tasks.

MF-Unit is obtained by inductive representation of local feature maps on different scales using sliding windows with different perceptual fields, containing rich local information representing category-consistent characteristics.
MF-Unit is calculated via inductive max and mean operations on each sliding window to compress parameters and reduce redundancy, representing category-consistent features with inductive knowledge.

During inference, MF-Adapter first infers test images into MF-Units at different levels and scales, retrieves few-shot knowledge in the MF-Unit space of the support set to get local logits, then combines this with the original CLIP high-level prediction for the final prediction.
MF-Adapter achieves state-of-the-art performance across 11 widely adopted datasets for few-shot classification, and is the first work to utilize the local similarity of CLIP in few-shot learning.

claim_records.text: The proposed subspace representation learning (SRL) framework represents an image using a subspace in local CNN feature space and measures similarity between two images via a weighted subspace distance (WSD).
When K images are available per class, the SRL framework develops two types of template subspaces to aggregate K-shot information: the prototypical subspace (PS) and the discriminative subspace (DS).
The SRL framework extends metric learning based techniques from vector to subspace representation.
Using subspace representation instead of the previously adopted global vector representation can effectively preserve the spatial structure and diversity within an image.

claim_records.text: Experimental results on three public benchmark datasets (MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB)) demonstrate competitive or superior performance of the SRL method compared to previous state-of-the-art approaches.

claim_records.text: Metric-based few-shot image classification directly measures relations between query images and support classes to learn transferable feature embeddings.
Previous work using image-level feature representations cannot effectively estimate a class's distribution due to the scarcity of samples.
Local descriptor based representations can achieve richer representations than image-level based representations.

Existing local descriptor based few-shot learning works still rely on a less effective instance-level metric, especially a symmetric metric, to measure relations between query images and support classes.
An asymmetric measure is argued to be more suitable for metric-based few-shot learning given the natural asymmetric relation between a query image and a support class.

fact_fields.method: asymmetric measure for metric-based few-shot learning

claim_records.text: The proposed Asymmetric Distribution Measure (ADM) network calculates a joint local and global asymmetric measure between two multivariate local distributions of queries and classes for few-shot learning.
A task-aware Contrastive Measure Strategy (CMS) is proposed to further enhance the measure function in the ADM network.
On miniImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 3.02% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.
On tieredImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 1.56% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.

claim_records.text: RankDNN casts relevance ranking for image retrieval as binary ranking relation classification.
Ranking relation classification is sample efficient and domain agnostic in comparison to image classification.
The core component of RankDNN is a simple MLP that takes as input an image triplet encoded as the difference between two vector-Kronecker products, and outputs a binary relevance ranking order.
RankMLP can be built on top of any state-of-the-art feature extractors.
RankDNN can be flexibly fused with other post-processing methods.
During meta test, RankDNN ranks support images according to their similarity with the query samples, and each query sample is assigned the class label of its nearest neighbor.
RankDNN can effectively improve the performance of its baselines based on a variety of backbones.
RankDNN outperforms previous state-of-the-art algorithms on multiple few-shot learning benchmarks including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds, and CIFAR-FS.
Experiments on the cross-domain challenge demonstrate the superior transferability of RankDNN.

claim_records.text: Traditional metric-based few-shot classification methods typically rely on a single distance value between the query feature and support feature, overlooking the contribution of shallow features.

The proposed method uses a multi-output embedding network that maps samples into distinct feature spaces by extracting feature vectors at different stages, enabling the model to capture both global and abstract features.
Employing a self-attention mechanism improves the refinement of features at each stage, leading to more robust representations and improved overall performance.
Assigning learnable weights to each stage of the multi-output embedding network significantly improved performance and results.
Comprehensive evaluations of the proposed method were conducted on the MiniImageNet and FC100 datasets in the 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot scenarios.
Cross-domain tasks across eight benchmark datasets were performed for the proposed method, achieving high accuracy in the testing domains.
The evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in comparison to state-of-the-art approaches.
The goal of few-shot classification is to train a classifier using a limited number of samples while maintaining satisfactory performance.

claim_records.text: A measure at only the image feature level may not be effective enough to generalize from base to novel classes when using only a few images.
The proposed multi-level correlation network (MLCN) for few-shot image classification effectively captures local information by using a multi-level descriptor of an image.
The self-correlation module and cross-correlation module in MLCN learn the semantic correspondence relation of local information based on learned representations.
The pattern-correlation module in MLCN captures the pattern of fine-grained images and finds relevant structural patterns between base classes and novel classes.
Extensive experiments and analysis show the effectiveness of the proposed MLCN method on four widely-used few-shot image classification benchmarks.

claim_records.text: HyperShot is a proposed few-shot learning model that fuses kernels and the hypernetwork paradigm.
Unlike reference approaches that apply a gradient-based adjustment of parameters, HyperShot switches classification module parameters depending on the task's embedding.
HyperShot utilizes a hypernetwork that takes aggregated information from support data and returns classifier parameters handcrafted for the considered problem.
HyperShot introduces a kernel-based representation of support examples delivered to the hypernetwork to create the parameters of the classification module.
HyperShot relies on relations between embeddings of support examples instead of direct feature values provided by backbone models.
The HyperShot approach enables the model to adapt to highly different tasks.

claim_records.text: Two identified crucial advantages of contrastive learning compared to meta learning are comprehensive utilization of graph nodes and the power of graph augmentations.

COLA can utilize all nodes to construct meta-tasks, further reducing the risk of overfitting.

claim_records.text: The proposed Siamese Transformer Network (STN) employs two parallel branch networks utilizing the pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to extract global and local features respectively.
The STN implementation uses the ViT-Small network architecture, with branch networks initialized with pre-trained model parameters obtained through self-supervised learning.
The STN applies Euclidean distance measure to global features and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure to local features.
The STN integrates the two feature metrics by first applying L2 normalization then weighting the normalized results to obtain the final similarity score.
During the training phase, the STN adopts a meta-learning approach to fine-tune the entire network.

Extensive experiments show the STN framework achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on four popular few-shot classification benchmarks in both 5-shot and 1-shot scenarios.

claims: The presented spatial-relational few-shot image classification architecture has an ultra-lightweight parameter count ranging from 22,249 to 34,917.

Under the strictly matched iso-episode-budget protocol (250 meta-training episodes, 5 canonical seeds, 600 evaluation episodes per seed), the architecture achieves consistent 5-shot accuracy gains across all five seeds over Prototypical Networks, Relation Networks, and MAML on both CIFAR-FS and MiniImageNet.
The architecture uses 27-53% fewer parameters than any of the compared baselines (Prototypical Networks, Relation Networks, MAML).
The architecture converges in fewer training episodes than the compared baselines.
The architecture generalizes better to the unseen fine-grained CUB-200-2011 birds domain with zero retraining than the compared baselines.
The architecture is more robust to 50% occlusion than all three compared baselines.
The architecture is more robust to 25% spatial translation than all three compared baselines.

Falsification ablations (zeroing relational tokens at inference and retraining without them entirely) show the architecture's pairwise relational computation is not the primary driver of its performance; the content-adaptive patch locator is.
A capacity sweep shows a genuine accuracy plateau near 22-35k parameters for the architecture.

claim_records.text: The proposed Mutual Centralized Learning (MCL) method affiliates two disjoint sets of dense features in a bidirectional paradigm, associating each local feature with a particle that can bidirectionally random walk in a discrete feature space by the affiliations.
MCL estimates class probability via features' accessibility, which measures the expected number of visits to the support features of that class in a Markov process.
MCL relates to learning a centrality on an affiliation network and can be plugged into existing methods by highlighting centralized local features.
Experiments show that the MCL method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both miniImageNet and tieredImageNet.

claim_records.text: The proposed Generative Dual Adversarial Network provides a unified framework for visual->semantic mapping, semantic->visual mapping, and metric learning for generalized zero-shot learning.

The proposed model consists of a feature generator that generates visual features from class embeddings, a regressor that maps visual features back to class embeddings, and a discriminator that evaluates closeness between image features and class embeddings.
All three components of the proposed model are trained under the combination of cyclic consistency loss and dual adversarial loss.
Experimental results show the proposed model preserves higher accuracy in classifying images from seen classes compared to prior approaches.
Experimental results show the proposed model performs better than existing state-of-the-art models in classifying images from unseen classes.

claim_records.text: The proposed patch-driven relational refinement learns cache adapter weights from intra-image patch dependencies rather than treating an image embedding as a monolithic vector.

The introduced relational gated graph attention network constructs a patch graph and performs edge-aware attention to emphasize informative inter-patch interactions, producing context-enriched patch embeddings.
A learnable multi-aggregation pooling composes context-enriched patch embeddings into compact, task-discriminative representations that better align cache keys with the target few-shot classes.
The proposed graph refinement is used only during training to distil relational structure into the cache, incurring no additional inference cost beyond standard cache lookup.
Final predictions are obtained by a residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits.

claim_records.text: Few-shot Cosine Transformer (FS-CT) consists of a learnable prototypical embedding network to obtain categorical representations from support samples with hard cases, and a transformer encoder to effectively achieve the relational map from two different support and query samples.

Cosine Attention, a more robust and stable attention module, enhances the transformer module significantly and improves FS-CT performance from 5% to over 20% in accuracy compared to the default scaled dot-product mechanism.
FS-CT performs competitive results in mini-ImageNet, CUB-200, and CIFAR-FS on 1-shot learning and 5-shot learning tasks across backbones and few-shot configurations.
A custom few-shot dataset for Yoga pose recognition was developed to demonstrate the potential of the FS-CT algorithm for practical application.
FS-CT with cosine attention is a lightweight, simple few-shot algorithm applicable for a wide range of applications such as healthcare, medical, and security surveillance.

claim_records.text: HelixFormer is a Transformer-based double-helix model proposed to achieve cross-image object semantic relation mining in a bidirectional and symmetrical manner for few-shot fine-grained image classification.
HelixFormer consists of two steps: Relation Mining Process (RMP) across different branches, and Representation Enhancement Process (REP) within each individual branch.

The designed RMP in HelixFormer enables each branch to extract fine-grained object-level Cross-image Semantic Relation Maps (CSRMs) using information from the other branch, ensuring better cross-image interaction in semantically related local object regions.

With the aid of CSRMs, the developed REP in HelixFormer strengthens extracted features for discovered semantically-related local regions in each branch, boosting the model's ability to distinguish subtle feature differences of fine-grained objects.

Extensive experiments on five public fine-grained benchmarks demonstrate that HelixFormer achieves much better performance over most state-of-the-art methods under 1-shot and 5-shot few-shot scenarios.
The code for HelixFormer is publicly available at https://github.com/JiakangYuan/HelixFormer.

claim_records.text: In few-shot learning, the conventional pooled global feature is likely to lose useful local characteristics.

Existing deep descriptor-based FSL methods generally take all deep descriptors from neural networks into consideration, ignoring that some descriptors are useless in classification due to their limited receptive field.

The paper argues that a Mutual Nearest Neighbor (MNN) relation should be established to explicitly select query descriptors most relevant to each task and discard less relevant ones from aggregative clutters in FSL.
The proposed method for FSL is Discriminative Mutual Nearest Neighbor Neural Network (DMN4).

claim_records.text: Extensive experiments demonstrate that DMN4 outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on both fine-grained and generalized datasets.

Extensive experiments carried on inductive FSL tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the COSOC approach.

claim_records.text: FiT combines fixed pretrained backbones, fine-tuned FiLM adapter layers, automatically configured Naive Bayes classifiers, and episodic training to produce parameter efficient image classification models with superior low-shot classification accuracy.
FiT achieves better classification accuracy than the leading Big Transfer (BiT) algorithm at low-shot across a wide range of downstream datasets.
FiT achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the challenging VTAB-1k benchmark using fewer than 1% of the updateable parameters.

FiT demonstrates parameter efficiency and superior accuracy in distributed low-shot applications including model personalization and federated learning where model update size is an important performance metric.
The parameter efficiency of FiT enables few-shot learning, inexpensive model updates for personalization, and communication efficient federated learning.

claim_records.text: Most current few shot methods train an encoder on a base dataset rich in labeled examples to obtain representations of support instances for novel classes, but test instances from a distribution different to the base distribution have poor feature representation quality that degrades performance.

BaseTransformers attends to the most relevant regions of the base dataset feature space and improves support instance representations by using well-trained feature representations of base dataset points closest to each support instance during meta-test time.
Experiments on three benchmark datasets show that BaseTransformers works well for several backbones and achieves state-of-the-art results in the inductive one shot setting.

claim_records.text: In meta-learning for few-shot classification, the shot number used during meta-training generally should match the shot number used during meta-testing to obtain the best performance.
The paper introduces a theoretical analysis of the impact of shot number on Prototypical Networks, a state-of-the-art few-shot classification method.
The proposed method derived from the theoretical analysis is robust to the choice of shot number used during meta-training, which is identified as a crucial hyperparameter.
The model trained for an arbitrary meta-training shot number shows great performance across different values of meta-testing shot numbers.
The approach is experimentally demonstrated on different few-shot classification benchmarks.

claim_records.text: Prototypical Random Walk Networks (PRWN) is a semi-supervised few-shot learning approach built on top of Prototypical Networks (PN).
The developed random walk semi-supervised loss enables the network to learn representations that are compact and well-separated.

Compact and well-separated class representations can be achieved by modeling the prototypical random walk notion without needing additional graph-NN parameters or requiring a transductive setting where a collective test set is provided.
The PRWN model outperforms baselines in most benchmarks, with significant improvements in some cases.

PRWN trained with 40% of the data as labeled achieves 50.89% accuracy in the 1-shot mini-Imagenet case, outperforming fully supervised Prototypical Networks trained on 100% of the labels which achieves 49.4% accuracy.

fact_fields.method: PRWN vs fully supervised Prototypical Networks

claim_records.text: The PRWN loss is resistant to distractors, which are unlabeled data that do not belong to any of the training classes, reflecting robustness to labeled/unlabeled class distribution mismatch.

fact_fields.method: Observation of existing few-shot hyperspectral image classification methods' classification results

claim_records.text: The proposed APNT method takes the prototype network as the backbone and adopts a transformer as feature extractor to learn pixel-to-pixel relation and apply different attentions to different pixels.
APNT randomly mixes up two patches to imitate boundary patches and uses the synthetic patches for training, to enlarge the number of hard training samples and enhance their diversity.
APNT follows the TransMix data augmentation technique, using the attention returned by the transformer to mix up the labels of two patches to generate better labels for synthetic patches.
The proposed APNT method demonstrates state of the art performance and better robustness for few-shot hyperspectral image classification compared with existing methods in experiments.
Few-shot hyperspectral image classification aims to identify the classes of each pixel in hyperspectral images by only marking few of these pixels.
Fixed-size patches centering around each pixel are often used for few-shot hyperspectral image classification to obtain spatial-spectral joint features of each pixel.

claim_records.text: Proto-CLIP is a few-shot learning framework that leverages large-scale vision-language models such as CLIP, utilizing both image prototypes and text prototypes for few-shot learning.
Proto-CLIP adapts the image and text encoder embeddings from CLIP in a joint fashion using few-shot examples.
The embeddings from CLIP's image and text encoders are used to compute the respective prototypes of image classes for classification in Proto-CLIP.

During adaptation, Proto-CLIP aligns the image and text prototypes of corresponding classes, which is beneficial for few-shot classification due to reinforced contributions from both types of prototypes.
Proto-CLIP has both training-free and fine-tuned variants.
The effectiveness of Proto-CLIP is demonstrated by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets for few-shot learning, as well as in the real world for robot perception.
